messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Kofi is a 23-year-old urban planner who came to therapy at the urging of his supervisor, after months of declining performance and a growing pattern of isolation. The event that shattered his sense of safety happened eighteen months ago, late one evening after a community engagement meeting in a neighborhood he was helping to redevelop. A group of men, drunk and angry about the planned changes, had cornered him in the parking lot. One of them threw a half-empty bottle that smashed against the wall beside his head, while another screamed in his face, his breath thick with alcohol. Kofi froze, unable to move or speak, certain he was going to be beaten or killed. A security guard eventually intervened, but by then the damage was done.

In the weeks that followed, Kofi found he could not shake the memory. It came to him not as a story he could tell, but as a series of vivid, frozen snapshots: the bottle arcing through the headlights, the man’s contorted face, the sour smell of beer. When these images surfaced, he became so overwhelmed by a wave of pure terror that he would have to stop whatever he was doing, his mind going blank, unable to find any words for what he had experienced. He began to avoid any situation that might involve disagreement. At work, he stopped voicing opinions in meetings, even when his input was critical to a project. He had come to believe that the institutions that should have protected him—his own city’s police, the security company at the site—had let him down, and that this proved he could not rely on anyone. This conviction deepened his sense of helplessness; he was certain that he could not stop bad things from happening to him, and that even the slightest upset would now be more than he could handle.

The smell of alcohol became a powerful trigger. One evening at a bar with colleagues, a man at the next table laughed loudly and gestured with his beer, and Kofi felt his heart pound so hard he thought he might pass out. The sound of the bottle clinking against the table was enough to send the snapshot memory flooding back. He fled to the bathroom, trembling, and spent the rest of the night convinced he was not safe. Even when his friends told him the bar was fine, he found it impossible to believe them. He started jumping at ordinary sounds—a door slamming, a car backfiring—and any unexpected movement nearby made him react as if he were about to be attacked. These moments of hypervigilance and fear would themselves trigger the memory again, locking him in a loop where threat and recollection fed each other.

To cope, Kofi began to gamble. He would drive to a casino on weekends, losing himself in the flashing lights and the noise, the thrill of the bet providing a temporary escape from the dread that followed him. But the relief never lasted. The next day, he would wake up feeling worse, dwelling on what he had done wrong—why he had frozen that night, why he was so weak now. This self-blame rumination only reinforced his belief that he could not cope, which in turn made him more vigilant for threats. The gambling itself became a new source of shame, and the shame triggered more memories, more avoidance, more fear. He stopped going to the bar entirely. He began taking the longest route to work to avoid the neighborhood where the assault happened, and he screened his calls to avoid any conversation that might turn confrontational. His supervisor noticed he was no longer contributing to team discussions, and his once-promising career trajectory stalled.

What finally brought Kofi to therapy was a panic attack during a routine zoning board hearing, triggered by a resident who calmly but firmly expressed anger about a proposed development. The man did not shout, but his tone was sharp, and Kofi felt the familiar surge of terror. He excused himself, went to the bathroom, and sat on the floor, shaking, unable to breathe. He knew he could not keep living this way. What frightens him most now is the thought that he will never feel safe again, and that the person he was before that night is gone for good.
